screeningScope: Full-text source, eligibility, study-design, taxonomy, and synthesis-readiness review of queue positions 1-12 after Batch 11 publication.

decisionDefinitions.INCLUDE: Eligible for evidence extraction and synthesis after full-text review.
decisionDefinitions.DEGRADED: A required source or verification element was unavailable.

records.sourceFile: Recovery of the autonomic nervous system following football training among Division I collegiate football athletes - The influence of intensity and time.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Fifty male Division I football players wore ECG-capable armbands across 128 training sessions during a 25-week season. Longer time at the highest heart-rate thresholds was associated with higher resting heart rate and slower heart-rate recovery the next day, with stronger associations at 150 and 160 bpm than at lower intensity.
records.limitations: The study measured recovery at 24 hours but could not identify the full recovery window, observed one male football program, and did not control nutrition, hydration, sleep, or recovery treatments. It was observational, and several authors reported financial relationships with the monitoring-device company.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the findings to support individualized recovery surveillance and session planning, not as proof that a universal heart-rate threshold causes under-recovery or that one device measure should dictate training.

records.sourceFile: Recreational and ergogenic substance use and substance use disorders in elite athletes- a narrative review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: The narrative review found that alcohol, cannabis, tobacco, prescribed opioids, and stimulants were commonly reported among elite athletes, usually at lower rates than non-athletes, while binge alcohol, oral tobacco, non-prescription opioids, and anabolic-androgenic steroids appeared higher in some athlete groups, especially power and collision sports.
records.limitations: The review found no prevalence studies of diagnosed substance-use disorders in elite athletes and few direct comparison groups. Prevalence estimates varied by country, sport, sex, competitive level, definitions, self-report, and detection method; the narrative method did not provide a pooled estimate or formal certainty rating.
records.synthesisCaution: Use confidential, clinically governed screening and referral rather than stereotypes, punitive inference, or diagnosis from a single disclosure. Supplement and medication discussions also require current antidoping verification.

records.sourceFile: Protect the player, protect the game - Reflections from ex-professional rugby union players on law changes, protective equipment, and duty of care in the professional game.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Interviews with 23 retired professional male rugby-union players, 61% of whom had played internationally, identified pressure to play with concussion symptoms, manipulation of concussion tests, and a preference for objective medical decision-making, longer return-to-play processes, less contact exposure, and continuing duty of care after retirement.
records.limitations: This retrospective qualitative sample was small, male, self-selected, and retired within the previous decade. Recall and social-desirability biases are possible, and changes in laws, workload, and concussion management since retirement may limit transfer to current players.
records.synthesisCaution: Treat the accounts as evidence about culture and safeguards, not prevalence estimates. Medical independence, protected disclosure, and conservative concussion management should not depend on protective equipment claims alone.

records.sourceFile: Relative training load and match outcome - Are professional soccer players actually undertrained during the in-season.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: GPS data from 21 professional soccer players across 67 training sessions and 14 matches linked match outcome with the week's training-to-match ratios. Winning was associated with more high-intensity running three days before the match, more volume five days before it, and less running, acceleration, and deceleration volume on the final two days.
records.limitations: Only one team was observed, the analysis was correlational, and match result is influenced by opponent, tactics, player availability, and many unmeasured factors. Included players had to complete full training and the subsequent match, and internal load was not measured.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the weekly pattern as a hypothesis for local periodization, not evidence that a prescribed training-to-match ratio will cause a win. Evaluate individual readiness, schedule, tactics, and cumulative exposure.

records.sourceFile: Residual deficits in reactive strength indicate incomplete restoration of athletic qualities following ACL reconstruction in professional soccer players.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Seventy-three soccer players at the end of ACL-reconstruction rehabilitation and 195 matched controls completed a 10-second single-leg vertical hop test. The ACLR group retained between-limb deficits and greater asymmetry; single-leg drop-jump reactive strength and knee-extension torque explained part of rebound height and reactive-strength performance.
records.limitations: The cross-sectional design lacked preinjury values and cannot show whether the deficits predict reinjury or failed return. A control comparison does not establish individual readiness, and predictive models explained only part of performance variance.
records.synthesisCaution: Add repeated vertical rebound testing to a multidomain return-to-sport battery when measurement quality is adequate, but do not substitute one symmetry score for symptoms, strength, movement strategy, conditioning, confidence, and soccer exposure.

records.sourceFile: The distribution of match activities relative to the maximal intensities in elite soccer players - Implications for practice.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Across 46 Serie A matches and 680 player-match samples, 90-minute average locomotor intensity was far below each player's one-minute match peak, especially for sprinting, acceleration, and deceleration. Time and distance above the match average and positional differences showed why an average-only benchmark can miss meaningful high-intensity exposure.
records.limitations: Match peaks are not the same as each athlete's maximal capacity. Internal load, counts of high-intensity actions, directional changes, location, opponent quality, congestion, and seasonal period were not analyzed, limiting individual prescription.
records.synthesisCaution: Use average, above-average, peak, position, and individual-capacity references together. Do not turn a one-minute match peak into a universal training target or assume reproducing locomotor load reproduces total match demand.

records.sourceFile: Is additive manufacturing improving performance in sports - A systematic review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: The review included 26 articles across 12 sports. Ten reported better performance for additively manufactured products than conventional comparators, eight reported similar performance, and five reported lower performance; most applications were isolated studies, and key printer or design-software details were often missing.
records.limitations: Evidence through May 2019 was sparse, heterogeneous, and unsuitable for a pooled effect. Many studies had small samples or laboratory outcomes, long-term durability and field transfer were uncertain, and incomplete manufacturing reporting limited replication.
records.synthesisCaution: Require sport-specific fit, safety, durability, regulatory, and performance validation before adoption. Customization and engineering plausibility are not evidence that a printed product improves athlete outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Is melatonin as an ergogenic hormone a myth - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Twenty-one studies entered the systematic review and 19 the meta-analysis. Melatonin did not improve time-trial, oxygen-uptake, or strength performance; among pooled recovery biomarkers, glutathione peroxidase increased, while exercise itself did not consistently change postexercise melatonin secretion.
records.limitations: The evidence base was small, and some participants contributed more than one outcome or trial. Doses, timing, performance tests, recovery markers, and populations varied, so the authors advised caution despite concluding that some recovery markers improved.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not recommend melatonin as an ergogenic aid or infer broad recovery benefit from one antioxidant marker. Sleep complaint, travel, dose, timing, side effects, interactions, product quality, and medical oversight require individual review.

records.sourceFile: Is there rationale for the cuff pressures prescribed for blood flow restriction exercise - A systematic review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Fifty-one BFR-exercise studies individualized pressure from measured limb or arterial occlusion, but prescribed values still ranged from 30% to 100% of occlusion pressure and only seven study applications provided a rationale for the selected percentage. Equipment and methodology also varied substantially.
records.limitations: The review focused on pressure-selection rationale and did not compare training outcomes across pressures. Differences in populations, cuff systems, width, material, exercise modes, and reporting prevent identification of an ideal pressure.
records.synthesisCaution: Measure occlusion with the actual cuff and position, use the lowest justified individualized stimulus, document equipment and response, and screen contraindications. The review does not support one universal percentage or unsupervised use.

records.sourceFile: Isometric training and long -term   adaptations; effects of muscle length, intensity and intent- A systematic   review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Across 23 research outputs lasting at least three weeks, longer-muscle-length isometrics generally produced greater hypertrophy and transfer than shorter-length work, ballistic intent favored rapid force production, and contractions at or above 70% MVC appeared necessary for meaningful tendon adaptation. Maximal force and hypertrophy improved across intensities.
records.limitations: Few studies directly compared prescription variables, protocols and outcomes were highly varied, and dynamic or closed-chain transfer, fatigue, rehabilitation populations, free-weight applications, and long-term combinations with dynamic training were sparsely studied.
records.synthesisCaution: Match joint angle, intent, intensity, volume, and pain tolerance to the target adaptation. The review supports specificity principles, not a single optimal isometric protocol for every athlete or tissue.

records.sourceFile: Optimizing Agility Training in Team Sport Players—The Role of Perception-Action Coupling - A Systematic Review with Multi-Level Meta-Analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Twenty-eight team-sport studies were included and 26 contributed 53 effects after influential-study exclusions. Perception-action agility training improved reactive-agility tests by a large pooled effect and preplanned tests by a moderate effect, while reaction-test improvement was not significant; favorable studies commonly lasted seven to eight weeks.
records.limitations: Reactive-agility evidence had moderate certainty and secondary outcomes low or very low certainty, with substantial within-study heterogeneity and possible publication or outcome-reporting bias. Soccer and basketball dominated, female athletes were underrepresented, and training load and retention were poorly reported.
records.synthesisCaution: Train perception and action together with representative stimuli, but treat the reported seven-to-eight-week, high-frequency pattern as a descriptive cluster rather than a proven optimum. Monitor total load and preserve sport specificity.

records.sourceFile: Qualitative and quantitative situational characteristics of muscle strains in sports - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Twenty-one video-analysis studies described 728 indirect or non-contact muscle injuries. Seventy-four percent were non-contact and almost half running-related; muscle-specific patterns involved active force production during rapid length change, including late-swing running for many hamstrings and distinct kicking, reaching, and sport-specific actions for other groups.
records.limitations: Football and hamstring injuries dominated, female athletes and other muscle groups were underrepresented, study quality ranged from low to high, terminology and methods differed, and video source, quality, rater expertise, or population were sometimes poorly reported. Video can describe situations but cannot establish a single causal mechanism.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the patterns to improve representative preparation and clinical questioning, not to claim that one joint position caused an injury. Muscle- and sport-specific prevention proposals still require prospective trial evidence.
